etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English difficult (ca. 1400), a back-formation from difficultee (whence modern difficulty), from Old French difficulté, from Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile. Replaced native Middle English earveþ (“difficult, hard”), from Old English earfoþe (“difficult, laborious, full of hardship”), cognate to German Arbeit (“work”).

definitions.definition: Hard, not easy, requiring much effort.

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, chapter 17, in The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: There is not the strength or courage left me to venture into the wide, strange, difficult world, alone.

quote.citation: 2008, Daniel Goleman, Destructive Emotions: A Scientific Dialogue with the Dalai Lama, →ISBN, page 199:
quote.text: In adults, the same kind of anger has been studied in people trying to solve a very difficult math problem. Though the tough math problem is very frustrating, there is an active attempt to solve the problem and meet the goal.

quote.citation: 2013 August 3, “Boundary problems”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8847:
quote.text: Economics is a messy discipline: too fluid to be a science, too rigorous to be an art. Perhaps it is fitting that economists’ most-used metric, gross domestic product (GDP), is a tangle too. […] But as a foundation for analysis it is highly subjective: it rests on difficult decisions about what counts as a territory, what counts as output and how to value it. Indeed, economists are still tweaking it.

definitions.definition: (often of a person, or a horse, etc) Hard to manage, uncooperative, troublesome.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling:
quote.text: “I hope, madam,” said Jones, “my charming Lady Bellaston will be as difficult to believe anything against one who is so sensible of the many obligations she hath conferred upon him.”

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To make difficult; to impede; to perplex.

quote.citation: August 9 1678,  William Temple, letter to Joseph Williamson
quote.text: their Excellencies having desisted from their pretensions , which had difficulted the peace
